supplementary_news.content: In August 2024, the WHO declared the mpox upsurge in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and its spread to neighboring countries, a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. The emergence of a new strain and its rapid spread across eastern DRC, and later to other African countries and beyond, made reliable diagnosis essential for understanding the scale of the epidemic and guide vaccination and other public health measures. A study led by the University of Geneva (UNIGE), the Institute of Tropical Medicine Antwerp (Belgium) and the National Institute of Biomedical Research (DRC), analyzed more than 2,700 PCR results for mpox in four Congolese cities — Goma, Kamituga, Kinshasa, and Uvira — between April 2024 and April 2026. The findings show that 35% of samples reported as PCR-positive may not have represented true infections, but rather environmental contamination with mpox viral DNA. Published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases , the study has direct implications for outbreak surveillance and for the individuals falsely diagnosed. Mpox is a viral disease characterised by fever and a distinctive rash that can cause painful and disfiguring skin lesions and, in some cases, serious or fatal complications. Fast, reliable case detection is essential for measuring the scale of an outbreak, targeting vaccination, adjusting public health measures, and slowing transmission — particularly in resource-limited settings. PCR testing plays a central role in mpox diagnosis as clinical symptoms are not specific to this virus. But when the same unusual pattern emerged in results from several different treatment centres, the team led by Andrew Azman, associate professor at the Institute of Global Health and the Center for Emerging Viral Diseases at the UNIGE Faculty of Medicine, took notice. Instead of a continuous distribution of CT values (the indicator reflecting the amount of virus detected in a sample — the lower the value, the higher the viral load ), the results clustered sharply into two distinct groups. The first group corresponds to low values, consistent with a high viral load and therefore a genuine active infection. The second cluster sat just at the detection threshold, pointing to an extremely low viral load — atypical for a real infection, but typical of a residual viral trace. What's striking is that this clear split between the two groups appeared almost identically across all four sites, which is unlikely to be a coincidence." Andrew Azman, Associate Professor, Institute of Global Health and the Center for Emerging Viral Diseases, UNIGE Faculty of Medicine Contaminated surfaces To understand why, the team swabbed surfaces in the treatment areas of two care centres. Many of the surfaces tested positive for traces of the virus, while surfaces sampled outside the treatment areas came back negative. Mpox DNA is highly stable and can persist for several weeks on surfaces, or even remain in the air of treatment centres. This environmental contamination can then be picked up by mistake when sampling other patients, with no connection to an actual infection. "We also looked at serological data for these individuals where available," explains Megan O'Driscoll, the study's first author and a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Global Health. "89% of the people that our model predicts had false-positive diagnoses showed no trace of antibodies against the virus." In a small separate study, the team tested samples from patients with suspected mpox for multiple rash-causing viruses and found that most people had other viruses, like varicella ( chickenpox ) and measles, with few testing positive for mpox. Adjusting positivity threshold These false diagnoses carry real consequences — for public health resource allocation, and for the people affected: unnecessary overtreatment, hospitalisation, or quarantine at a mpox treatment centre, along with the social stigma associated with the disease, and a very real risk of contracting an actual infection there. "The simplest and fastest fix is to lower the PCR positivity threshold," Azman adds. "A lower threshold significantly reduces the number of false positives without meaningfully increasing false negatives — a proposal currently under discussion with decision-makers. In the long term, this shows that we need to improve the training of lab staff in low-resource settings like this so they can spot these anomalies in real time, rather than after the acute emergency is over." This work is part of the mandate of the Geneva Center for Emerging Viral Diseases, a WHO collaborating centre for diagnostics, which supports several countries in improving their diagnostic practices. Source: Journal reference: O’Driscoll, M., et al . (2026). The risk of mpox false positive results in high transmission settings: evidence from a multi-site observational study in DR Congo. The Lancet Infectious Diseases . DOI: 10.1016/S1473-3099(26)00411-1. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1473309926004111?via%3Dihub

supplementary_news.content: News Health Mpox case confirmed in Bunia amid Ebola outbreak — TimesLIVE UA.NEWS 26 September 2026 12:00 In the city of Bunia in the northeast of the Democratic Republic of Congo, a case of mpox has been laboratory-confirmed in a 21-year-old woman. She went to hospital on Thursday with a rash all over her body characteristic of the disease and received a positive test result on Friday, TimesLIVE reports, citing the head of the local hospital, Davin Ambitapio Musungufu, and health system representatives. Patients isolated Another woman, aged 32, is a suspected mpox case. She is awaiting laboratory test results. Both patients have been isolated and are being cared for by a separate medical team. According to Musungufu, medics are identifying the confirmed patient's contacts and trying to determine the source of the infection. Doctor Adelar Lofungola, who was deputy head of the mpox response in the DRC, said that five suspected cases of the disease are also being investigated in Bunia. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Strain due to Ebola Bunia is located in Ituri province, where an Ebola outbreak was declared on May 15. According to government data released on Thursday, 7,890 people were infected and 3,799 died during this outbreak. Mpox is a viral disease that causes fever and skin lesions and is transmitted through close physical contact. In April, the DRC lifted the public health emergency status for mpox after a three-year outbreak during which more than 34,000 cases were confirmed in the country. At the time, authorities warned that the virus had not been eliminated and could spread again. Lofungola noted that over the past month, medics have recorded an increase in mpox cases in several parts of the country. According to him, the Ebola outbreak complicates the monitoring of other infections because of the strain on the healthcare system. Read us on Download our app

supplementary_news.content: Sunday, September 27, 2026 News Crime and Courts South Africa Africa World BRICS Education Energy Environment Feel Good Government at Work Opinion Politics Opinion Opinion News Politics Entertainment Lifestyle Tech Sport Business Jobs Economy Property Window on China Hybrid Working Entertainment Celebrity News Streaming Movies Music Books Whats On Joburg Durban Cape Town Pretoria Opinion Lifestyle Health Beauty Fashion Food Relationships Parenting Competitions Opinion Travel Local International Tech Software and Internet Esports Opinion Sport Soccer PSL Rugby Cricket MMA Betting Opinion Horse Racing Motoring Reviews Launches Industry News Motorsport Cape Argus News Mpox alert: Western Cape traces contacts after cases linked to two gatherings Staff Reporter|Published 1 week ago Ask AI 2min Health officials are tracing contacts after two Western Cape gatherings were linked to mpox cases. Image: File Western Cape Health officials are trying to track down people who attended two gatherings in the province after people infected with mpox came into close contact with others. The warning comes as the Western Cape accounts for 15 of South Africa’s 18 confirmed mpox cases, with most of the province’s infections recorded in Cape Town. “There were two events, exposure events, that basically did lead to these Mpox cases,” Western Cape health department official Ednah Baloyi said. Health teams are now tracing people who were at the gatherings, testing those who may have been exposed and making sure anyone who tests positive receives treatment. “We are working very hard to make sure that those two clusters are, or rather the contacts that were involved in that exposure event are followed up, tested, and treated timeously when they’re found to be Mpox positive,” Baloyi said. Symptoms to watch for The new details come as health authorities try to stop further infections following a sharp increase in cases over the past month. South Africa had recorded 18 confirmed cases and one probable case by September 17. Thirteen cases were recorded between August 13 and September 17, an increase the National Department of Health said pointed to the virus being passed between people locally. Those affected are between 23 and 50 years old. Western Cape health officials are urging residents to watch for an unexplained rash, sores or skin lesions, particularly if they have been in close contact with someone who may have mpox. Other symptoms can include fever, headaches, muscle aches and tiredness. Mpox is mainly passed through close physical contact with an infected person, including contact with their skin lesions, scabs or body fluids. The virus can also be picked up from items such as bedding, clothing and towels used by an infected person. Video Player is loading. The infection is mainly spread through close physical contact with someone who has mpox. It can cause a rash, fever, swollen lymph nodes, headaches, muscle aches and tiredness. Most people recover from mpox within a few weeks, but the infection can cause more serious illness in some people. Here is what you need to know about mpox, including how it spreads, the symptoms to look out for, treatment and how to reduce your risk. What is Mpox? Mpox, previously known as monkeypox, is a viral disease caused by the monkeypox virus, which belongs to the Orthopoxvirus family. The infection commonly causes a rash or skin lesions, along with symptoms such as fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, tiredness and swollen lymph nodes. Mpox can occur in people of any age or background. There are different groups, or clades, of the virus. Clade I and Clade II have different patterns of circulation, but both can cause mpox in humans. This can include: Skin-to-skin contact with mpox lesions. Kissing and other close face-to-face contact. Sexual contact. Contact with bodily fluids or lesions. Contact with contaminated clothing, bedding, towels or other objects. Prolonged close contact involving respiratory particles. The virus can also spread from infected animals to people in areas where animal-to-human transmission occurs. Mpox is not generally spread as easily as common respiratory infections such as colds and flu. Close contact is an important route of transmission. What are the symptoms of Mpox? Symptoms can take time to appear after exposure. According to the World Health Organization, they can develop anywhere from one to 21 days after infection. Common symptoms include: Fever Headache Muscle aches Back pain Sore throat Tiredness Swollen lymph nodes A rash or skin lesions For some people, the rash is the first noticeable symptom. The illness often begins with general symptoms before the rash appears, although this is not always the case. Common symptoms include fever and headaches. Image: Diva Plavalaguna / Pexels What does the Mpox rash look like? The rash can appear on different parts of the body, including the face, hands, feet, mouth, groin and genital area. The lesions can change as the infection progresses, developing from flat spots into raised lesions, blisters and pus-filled lesions before crusting over and healing. They can be painful or itchy, and some people develop only a few lesions while others develop many. The rash can last for two to four weeks and may leave scars. Because mpox can resemble other illnesses and skin conditions, a rash should not be diagnosed based on appearance alone. Who is at greater risk of severe Mpox? Most people recover from mpox, but some groups have a higher risk of complications or severe illness. These include: Young children, particularly infants. Pregnant people. People with weakened immune systems. People living with poorly controlled HIV. People with certain other conditions that affect the immune system. Anyone who is concerned about their symptoms or has been exposed to someone with mpox should seek medical advice. How is Mpox diagnosed? Mpox can resemble conditions such as chickenpox, herpes, scabies and some bacterial skin infections, so symptoms alone may not be enough to confirm an infection. A healthcare professional can assess the symptoms and arrange testing where appropriate. Laboratory confirmation is generally done by testing material from a skin lesion, usually using a PCR test. A PCR test is used to determine if it's Mpox. Image: Cottonbro Studio / Pexels How is Mpox treated? There is no routine treatment that simply makes mild mpox disappear immediately. Treatment generally focuses on managing symptoms, looking after the skin, controlling pain and preventing complications or secondary infections. Most people recover without specific treatment within a few weeks. Specific antiviral medicines may be used in certain circumstances, particularly for people with severe illness or those at higher risk of complications. Their availability and use depend on local health systems and clinical guidance. What should you do if you think you have mpox? If you develop an unexplained rash, fever or other symptoms associated with mpox, particularly after close contact with someone who has the infection, contact a healthcare professional. Until you have been assessed, it is important to reduce the risk of passing the virus to other people. You should: Avoid close physical contact with other people. Avoid sharing towels, bedding, clothing and other personal items. Wash your hands regularly with soap and water or use hand sanitiser. Avoid touching or scratching lesions. Follow medical advice about staying away from other people while you are infectious. People with mpox can remain infectious until their lesions have healed and a new layer of skin has formed. Anyone can get Mpox Mpox is not limited to one particular group of people. Anyone who has close contact with an infected person can potentially become infected. Avoiding stigma is therefore important, as fear or embarrassment should not prevent someone from seeking medical care. If you think you may have been exposed to mpox or develop symptoms that could be consistent with the infection, speak to a healthcare professional for advice and testing. Mpox can resemble conditions such as chickenpox, herpes, scabies and some bacterial skin infections, so symptoms alone may not be enough to confirm an infection. A healthcare professional can assess the symptoms and arrange testing where appropriate. Laboratory confirmation is generally done by testing material from a skin lesion, usually using a PCR test. A PCR test is used to determine if it's Mpox. Image: Cottonbro Studio / Pexels How is Mpox treated? There is no routine treatment that simply makes mild mpox disappear immediately. Treatment generally focuses on managing symptoms, looking after the skin, controlling pain and preventing complications or secondary infections. Most people recover without specific treatment within a few weeks. Specific antiviral medicines may be used in certain circumstances, particularly for people with severe illness or those at higher risk of complications. Their availability and use depend on local health systems and clinical guidance. What should you do if you think you have mpox? If you develop an unexplained rash, fever or other symptoms associated with mpox, particularly after close contact with someone who has the infection, contact a healthcare professional. Until you have been assessed, it is important to reduce the risk of passing the virus to other people. You should: Avoid close physical contact with other people. Avoid sharing towels, bedding, clothing and other personal items. Wash your hands regularly with soap and water or use hand sanitiser. Avoid touching or scratching lesions. Follow medical advice about staying away from other people while you are infectious. People with mpox can remain infectious until their lesions have healed and a new layer of skin has formed. Anyone can get Mpox Mpox is not limited to one particular group of people. Anyone who has close contact with an infected person can potentially become infected. Avoiding stigma is therefore important, as fear or embarrassment should not prevent someone from seeking medical care. If you think you may have been exposed to mpox or develop symptoms that could be consistent with the infection, speak to a healthcare professional for advice and testing. Local Centre for Health Protection confirms mpox case and urges high-risk groups to vaccinate as cases rise By Edward Zhang - 11:14PM Thu September 24, 2026 188 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Pinterest Telegram 24th September 2026 – (Hong Kong) The Centre for Health Protection of the Department of Health said it is investigating a confirmed mpox case and appealed for heightened vigilance amid a recent upswing in infections. Officials strongly urged individuals who have had high-risk sexual contact, particularly with strangers, to adopt personal protective measures, including vaccination, and to avoid close physical contact with anyone suspected of infection. The authority stressed that unsafe sexual contact elevates the risk of transmission. close Advertisements dimsumdailyhk [custom chain] curation-20260924-09:13 CANCEL NEXT VIDEO play_arrow volume_mute AD PausePlay % buffered00:00 00:00 00:00 UnmuteMute Play The patient is a 36‐year‐old man who developed a fever and a perianal ulcer on 15th September. He attended a social hygiene service clinic on 18th September and was subsequently admitted to Princess Margaret Hospital for isolation. Laboratory testing by the Public Health Laboratory Services Branch detected the monkeypox virus, and he is in a stable condition. Based on the patient’s account, he had high-risk sexual exposure with other men in Hong Kong during the incubation period. The Centre for Health Protection has begun an epidemiological investigation and will report the case to the World Health Organisation. Health officials noted a sustained increase in cases since August. Since 2022, Hong Kong has logged 112 mpox infections, comprising 89 local and 23 imported cases, all in men. As of today, 28 cases have been recorded this year, including 22 local and six imported, with 19 reported since August. Investigations indicate all 19 recently identified patients engaged in high-risk sexual behaviours during the incubation period, including sex with male strangers or multiple partners and sex without a condom. Eleven patients used dating apps to find casual partners. Most were unvaccinated, and around 40 per cent were living with HIV. Genetic analysis found identical sequences in some infections, suggesting a common source and several transmission chains among men who have sex with men. Contact tracing has been hindered because some newly met partners could not be reached, prompting a call for the public to keep contact details for sexual partners to facilitate tracing when needed. To strengthen prevention and control, the Department of Health has launched targeted measures. An mpox hotline on 2125 2373 operates daily from 9.00am to 6.00pm to trace close contacts, provide health assessments and arrange vaccination. The Centre for Health Protection is working with non‐governmental organisations to deliver outreach vaccination and has intensified safer‐sex promotion in high-risk venues such as saunas. Operators of relevant dating apps are collaborating to push in‐app messages in Hong Kong on the risks of unsafe sexual contact and the benefits of vaccination. Vaccination is available for high-risk groups, including people with high-risk sexual practices such as having multiple partners, sex workers and individuals with a sexually transmitted infection within the past 12 months. Walk‐in mpox vaccinations are offered at Department of Health social hygiene service clinics in Chai Wan, Wan Chai (male and female), Yau Ma Tei (male and female), Yung Fung Shee, Fanling and Tuen Mun, as well as at the Yau Ma Tei Integrated Treatment Centre. The Kowloon Bay Integrated Treatment Centre and the Hospital Authority’s Special Medical Clinics at Queen Elizabeth Hospital and Princess Margaret Hospital also provide vaccination for their clients. In response to the case surge, an additional vaccination centre has been set up at the Centre for Health Protection Building, 147C Argyle Street, Mong Kok, for high-risk groups, who may call 2125 2373 to arrange their vaccination. supplementary_news.content: Mpox case confirmed in northeastern Congolese city at center of Ebola outbreak DAKAR, Sept 25 (Reuters) - A laboratory-confirmed case of mpox was identified in the northeastern Congolese city of Bunia, the director of a local hospital and two health officials said, raising concerns about a resurgence of the disease as the country battles its worst Ebola outbreak on record. • The epidemic caused by the Ebola outbreak was declared on May 15 in Ituri province, where Bunia is located, and has infected 7,890 people and killed 3,799, according to government data published on Thursday. • Mpox is a viral disease that causes fever and skin lesions and spreads through close physical contact. • Congo declared an end to mpox as a national public health emergency in April after a three-year outbreak that resulted in more than 34,000 confirmed cases nationwide. Authorities cautioned at the time that the virus had not been eradicated and could resurge. • The latest case involves a 21-year-old woman who was admitted to hospital on Thursday with lesions across her body consistent with mpox, hospital director Davin Ambitapio Musungufu said. She tested positive on Friday, he and two health officials told Reuters. • A second woman, aged 32, has been identified as a suspected mpox case and is awaiting laboratory results, Musungufu said. She and the confirmed patient have been isolated and are being cared for by a dedicated medical team. • Investigations are underway to trace contacts and identify the source of infection, Musungufu said. • Dr. Adelard Lofungola, a health official who served as deputy incident manager for Congo's mpox response, said five suspected mpox cases in Bunia were currently under investigation. • Health officials have reported an increase in mpox cases in several parts of the country over the past month, he said. • Lofungola said the Ebola outbreak's impact on Congo's health system was complicating efforts to monitor other infections. (Reporting and Writing by Clement Bonnerot; Editing by Bill Berkrot)

The emergence of a new strain and its rapid spread across eastern DRC, and later to other African countries and beyond, made reliable diagnosis essential for understanding the scale of the epidemic and guide vaccination and other public health measures. A study led by the University of Geneva (UNIGE), the Institute of Tropical Medicine Antwerp (Belgium) and the National Institute of Biomedical Research (DRC), analysed more than 2,700 PCR results for mpox in four Congolese cities — Goma, Kamituga, Kinshasa, and Uvira — between April 2024 and April 2026. The findings show that 35% of samples reported as PCR-positive may not have represented true infections, but rather environmental contamination with mpox viral DNA. Published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, the study has direct implications for outbreak surveillance and for the individuals falsely diagnosed. Mpox is a viral disease characterised by fever and a distinctive rash that can cause painful and disfiguring skin lesions and, in some cases, serious or fatal complications. Fast, reliable case detection is essential for measuring the scale of an outbreak, targeting vaccination, adjusting public health measures, and slowing transmission — particularly in resource-limited settings. PCR testing plays a central role in mpox diagnosis as clinical symptoms are not specific to this virus. But when the same unusual pattern emerged in results from several different treatment centres, the team led by Andrew Azman, associate professor at the Institute of Global Health and the Center for Emerging Viral Diseases at the UNIGE Faculty of Medicine, took notice. Instead of a continuous distribution of CT values (the indicator reflecting the amount of virus detected in a sample — the lower the value, the higher the viral load), the results clustered sharply into two distinct groups. "The first group corresponds to low values, consistent with a high viral load and therefore a genuine active infection," says Azman. "The second cluster sat just at the detection threshold, pointing to an extremely low viral load — atypical for a real infection, but typical of a residual viral trace. What's striking is that this clear split between the two groups appeared almost identically across all four sites, which is unlikely to be a coincidence." Contaminated surfaces To understand why, the team swabbed surfaces in the treatment areas of two care centres. Many of the surfaces tested positive for traces of the virus, while surfaces sampled outside the treatment areas came back negative. Mpox DNA is highly stable and can persist for several weeks on surfaces, or even remain in the air of treatment centres. This environmental contamination can then be picked up by mistake when sampling other patients, with no connection to an actual infection. "We also looked at serological data for these individuals where available," explains Megan O'Driscoll, the study's first author and a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Global Health. "89% of the people that our model predicts had false-positive diagnoses showed no trace of antibodies against the virus." In a small separate study, the team tested samples from patients with suspected mpox for multiple rash-causing viruses and found that most people had other viruses, like varicella (chickenpox) and measles, with few testing positive for mpox. Adjusting positivity threshold These false diagnoses carry real consequences — for public health resource allocation, and for the people affected: unnecessary overtreatment, hospitalisation, or quarantine at a mpox treatment centre, along with the social stigma associated with the disease, and a very real risk of contracting an actual infection there. "The simplest and fastest fix is to lower the PCR positivity threshold," Azman adds. "A lower threshold significantly reduces the number of false positives without meaningfully increasing false negatives — a proposal currently under discussion with decision-makers. In the long term, this shows that we need to improve the training of lab staff in low-resource settings like this so they can spot these anomalies in real time, rather than after the acute emergency is over." This work is part of the mandate of the Geneva Center for Emerging Viral Diseases, a WHO collaborating centre for diagnostics, which supports several countries in improving their diagnostic practices. https://www.unige.ch/medias/en/2026/mpox-plus-dun-tiers-des-tests-positifs-seraient-des-faux-diagnos... supplementary_news.content: Start Sport Switzerland International Football People MyTech Lifestyle Start Sport Switzerland International Football People MyTech Lifestyle NewsStudy: One in three positive Mpox tests could be a false positive Health Study: One in three positive Mpox test results could be a false positive The Mpox outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo led the WHO to declare an international public health emergency in August 2024. (File photo) Keystone A study from Geneva calls into question the reliability of Mpox PCR tests in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. According to the study, one in three positive Mpox test results may have been false. Keystone-SDA 23.09.2026, 08:50 For the study published in the journal *The Lancet Infectious Diseases*, an international research team led by the University of Geneva (Unige) analyzed more than 2,700 PCR tests for Mpox, the viral disease formerly known as monkeypox. The samples came from four cities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It was notable that the positive tests fell clearly into two groups: In one group, a large amount of viral material was detected—an indication of an actual infection. In the second group, however, only a tiny amount of viral DNA was present. According to the researchers, this suggested that the samples may have been contaminated by traces of the virus from the environment. According to the researchers, 35 percent of the positive samples fell into this second group and could therefore have been false-positive results. Viral DNA on Surfaces Studies conducted at two treatment centers provided a possible explanation. The researchers found Mpox DNA on numerous surfaces within the centers. This DNA could have accidentally been introduced into the samples during collection. Analysis of blood samples provided further evidence. In 89 percent of the individuals for whom the model suspected a false-positive diagnosis, no antibodies against the virus were detected. In a separate small study, the researchers also found that in many people with suspected mpox, other viruses—including the varicella and measles viruses—were the likely cause of the skin rashes. Consequences for Those Affected According to the study, false-positive diagnoses could have significant consequences. Those affected could be unnecessarily treated, hospitalized, or isolated in Mpox treatment centers. Furthermore, there is a risk of actual infection in those settings. False-positive test results could also distort the assessment of the infection situation when monitoring an outbreak and planning vaccinations. The researchers therefore propose that, going forward, only tests showing a stronger viral signal be classified as positive. In the long term, they also say that better training for laboratory staff is needed to detect unusual test patterns early on. Found an error? Picture: Guerchom Ndebo/WHO The health department has secured limited doses of Mpox vaccines as part of its response to local transmissions. 22 Mpox cases have been confirmed in parts of the country. This including 18 cases in the Western Cape, three in Gauteng, and one in Kwazulu-Natal. The department is urging anyone who has been in contact with a patient to seek immediate treatment. The viral infection may cause a painful rash or sores, fever and swollen glands. It can spread through close physical contact with an infected person, including sexual contact. During a global outbreak in 2022, South Africa formally recorded it's first case. Another resurgence occurred in 2024 with 25 cases and three deaths. The current cases includes a 47-year-old Cape Town resident who tested positive after his return from Spain. A German and Norwegian citizen have also tested positive. All patients except one are male. There are just over 500 Mpox vaccines in Gauteng kept in special freezers, while outbreak response teams continue to monitor transmission clusters. Helen Wallace Health, South Africa [Image: ChatGPT] Concerns about Mpox in South Africa have gone from “who cares?” to “maybe I should exercise some caution” as the number of cases has now risen from 18 to 22 as of Monday, with the majority of those infected being in the Western Cape, IOL reports. One of the newer cases is a 47-year-old Cape Town man who travelled to Spain earlier this month. He’d initially been listed as a probable case while health authorities waited on his lab results from Spain – those have since come back positive, and he’s now counted among the confirmed cases. The other three recent cases include two people who picked up infections abroad, a German national and a Norwegian national. Of the 22 confirmed cases nationally, 18 are in the Western Cape, three in Gauteng, and one in KwaZulu-Natal. Only one of the patients is a woman. Mpox can affect anyone, with symptoms that include fever, headaches, muscle aches, back pain, fatigue, and skin rashes or lesions. Anyone noticing these symptoms in themselves is urged to get medical attention quickly. Health Department spokesperson Foster Mohale said the department is working alongside the National Institute for Communicable Diseases, the World Health Organization and other partners to help the Western Cape roll out its response, including contact tracing and stepped-up surveillance. “Anyone who has been in close contact with a confirmed case within the past 21 days and develops symptoms should seek medical attention promptly,” Mohale said, urging people to flag their exposure history to healthcare providers. Mohale added that finding transmission clusters and cases spread across provinces shows why the public needs to keep cooperating, catching cases early and staying alert, and said the department would keep monitoring the situation and share updates as they come. While most cases are still concentrated in the Western Cape, if this escalates, the days of wearing a mask might be making a comeback. The department noted that the increase is as of 22 September 2026. The department’s Foster Mohale noted that a previous probable case has been added to the tally, after laboratory results confirmed the case of a 47-year-old man from Cape Town who returned from Spain earlier this month. “This individual was previously classified as a probable case pending laboratory results from Spanish health authorities. Following confirmation of a positive test, the case has been reclassified as laboratory-confirmed and included in the updated count,” said Mohale. He added that the other three cases include “two imported infections involving a German and a Norwegian citizen”. Meanwhile, the Western Cape still has the majority of the cases, now standing at 18, up from the initial 15 confirmed cases reported last week. The three cases in Gauteng and one in KwaZulu-Natal remain unchanged. All the patients are male except for one, Mohale said. At the same time, Mohale has reminded the public that early detection and cooperation are necessary to prevent further spread. “While most cases remain concentrated in the Western Cape, the identification of transmission clusters and cases across multiple provinces highlights the need for sustained public cooperation, early detection, and continued surveillance to prevent further spread,” said Mohale. Anyone who has been in contact with a confirmed case within the past 21 days and develops symptoms has been urged to immediately seek medical attention. Symptoms include: fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, fatigue, a rash/skin lesions on the face, hands, feet, genitals, or other areas of the body. The virus isn’t restricted to local transmission either; imported cases are driving some of these new numbers. A 47-year-old Capetonian recently returned from Spain to Cape Town with the virus. Three additional cases were identified in visiting Norwegian and German nationals. Where the cases are concentrated The majority of infections are clustered in the Western Cape, with 18 cases, while Gauteng has three cases and one case was recorded in KwaZulu-Natal. Almost every patient identified so far is male, with ages ranging from 23 to 50. In July, the Africa Centre for Disease Control and prevention donated more than 10 000 Mpox vaccines to the National Health Department. Read more Another woman killed in Ekurhuleni: 11th body found strangled in Springs Gauteng’s Health Department has assured it is ready to respond to Mpox. “Mpox vaccines are available with a total of 586 doses currently in stock. The vaccines are stored in dedicated freezers at regional pharmacies, from where clinics can request them,” it said on Tuesday. How to spot the symptoms early Mpox doesn’t always show up the same way in everyone, but it usually starts with flu-like warning signs before turning into distinct skin markings. Look out for high fever, pounding headaches and severe exhaustion, as well as deep muscle aches and persistent back pain. The giveaway signal of Mpox is a painful rash or raised fluid-filled lesions appearing on your face, hands, feet or intimate areas. RELATED ARTICLES Western Cape mass shooting leaves at least 10 dead and several injured 10th woman’s body found in Ekurhuleni: Here’s what the police revealed How it spreads (and how to protect yourself) Mpox relies heavily on close physical contact where it requires direct skin-to-skin contact with infected lesions or body fluids. However, it can also be picked up from shared items like unwashed bedding, towels or clothing that an infected person used. Health Department spokesperson Foster Mohale highlighted the urgency for anyone who thinks they might have been exposed. “Anyone who has been in close contact with a confirmed case within the past 21 days and develops symptoms should seek medical attention promptly and inform healthcare providers of their exposure history,” he cautioned. Mohale also stressed that while the Western Cape holds the primary cluster, scattered cases across other provinces mean everyone needs to be vigilant. “The identification of transmission clusters and cases across multiple provinces highlights the need for sustained public co-operation, early detection and continued surveillance to prevent further spread,” Mohale explained, adding that official channels will issue further updates as new data comes in. supplementary_news.content: Salt River, Cape Town 28 September 2026 WhatsApp 082 991 3913 Studio Line 021 442 3530 Follow Us Facebook X-twitter Youtube Instagram Tiktok Linkedin Whatsapp Shows View the Schedules Listen to the Podcasts News Local International News Opinions Sports News About Us VOCFM Team Salaah Times Contact Us search menuDonate search Search close close Showskeyboard_arrow_down View the Schedules Listen to the Podcasts Newskeyboard_arrow_down Local International News Opinions Sports News About Uskeyboard_arrow_down VOCFM Team Salaah Times Contact Us Showskeyboard_arrow_down View the Schedules Listen to the Podcasts Newskeyboard_arrow_down Local International News Opinions Sports News About Uskeyboard_arrow_down VOCFM Team Salaah Times Contact Us Team samnet More VOCFM News Local News Sports News Halaal News Opinions Tourism VOC Projects Local News Sports News Halaal News Opinions Tourism VOC Projects Western Cape expects more mpox cases as contact tracing continues Cape Town, Local, News, VOC News September 22, 2026 The Western Cape Department of Health and Wellness expects that more mpox cases could be identified as contact tracing continues following two social gatherings linked to a cluster in Cape Town. Speaking to VOC News, the department’s Chief Operating Officer, Dr Saadiq Karriem, said 13 of the province’s cases had been identified since mid-August and were linked to the two gatherings. “We were able to pick up a number of other people and tested them for mpox,” Karriem said. The latest National Institute for Communicable Diseases data shows that 21 mpox cases had been confirmed in South Africa by 18 September, with 17 reported in the Western Cape. Karriem said most cases have been mild and patients have been able to self-isolate at home. He said mpox spreads mainly through close physical contact, including contact with lesions, as well as contaminated clothing, bedding and other materials. “Most mpox cases are mild. They’ve been self-isolating at home where possible,” he said. Symptoms can include fever, headaches, muscle aches and swollen glands, followed by a rash or lesions that can appear on different parts of the body. Karriem said contact tracing is continuing, with health authorities working with the City of Cape Town, the NICD, the National Department of Health and the World Health Organisation to monitor cases and prevent further transmission. “Out of these cluster events, we’ll probably have a few more cases,” he said Photo: Pixabay Oyisa George Related Stories International Relations and Cooperation Minister Calls for UN Reform and Permanent African Representation 25 September 2026 Mosimane Confident Ahead of Guinea AFCON Qualifier 25 September 2026 Eskom 2.0: Ramokgopa Calls for Affordable and Sustainable Electricity 25 September 2026 Video Player is loading. 在Google 追踪《香港01》 讚好 1 1 0 0 0 0 卫生署卫生防护中心今(24日)表示,正调查一宗猴痘确诊个案,一名36岁男子本月15日出现发烧和肛门附近皮肤溃疡,至19日到卫生署辖下的社会卫生科诊所求医,获中心安排到玛嘉烈医院接受隔离治疗,目前情况稳定。其临床样本经中化验,证实对猴痘病毒呈阳性反应。据该病人提供资料,他于潜伏期内曾于香港与其他男子有高风险性接触。 中心指,留意到近期猴痘个案大幅上升,并强烈呼吁有高风险性接触人士(尤其与陌生人士)必需提高警觉,做好个人防护措施,包括接种猴痘疫苗。 卫生署卫生防护中心表示,留意到近期猴痘个案大幅上升,呼吁有高风险性接触人士(尤其与陌生人士)必需提高警觉,做好个人防护措施,包括接种猴痘疫苗。图示中心人员到访娱乐场所张贴宣传海报。(政府新闻处) 卫生防护中心正调查一宗猴痘确诊个案,个案涉及一名36岁男子,他本月15日出现发烧和肛门附近皮肤溃疡,19日到卫生署辖下的社会卫生科诊所求医,获中心安排到玛嘉烈医院接受隔离治疗,目前情况稳定。其临床样本经中化验,证实对猴痘病毒呈阳性反应。 据该病人提供资料,他於潜伏期内曾于香港与其他男子有高风险性接触。中心正继续就个案进行流行病学调查,亦会将个案通报世界卫生组织。 卫生防护中心。(资料图片) 中心指,留意到近期猴痘个案大幅上升,并强烈呼吁有高风险性接触人士(尤其与陌生人士)必需提高警觉,做好个人防护措施,包括接种猴痘疫苗,亦特别提醒不安全性接触会增加感染风险。 据中心的数据,截至今日,本年累计录得28宗个案,包括22宗本地个案及6宗输入个案,其中19宗为8月以来的新增个案。流行病学调查显示,近期发现的19宗个案中,所有患者报称在潜伏期内曾进行高风险性行为,大部份病人未曾接种猴痘疫苗。
